Midterm 2 crash course

Every section on Midterm 2, from §2.8 to §4.1, in 10 short lessons. Each lesson explains the idea, gives the recipe, and walks through examples one line at a time.

New: Midterm 2 comes from Quiz 3 and Quiz 4. Study the Quiz 3 & 4 review, then take the practice exam (52 points, 2 hours).

Midterm 2 is tomorrow, so this page is the shortest path through every section on it, from §2.8 to §4.1. Each lesson gives you:

  1. The idea in plain words: what the section is actually about.
  2. The recipe: the steps you follow on the exam, every time.
  3. Worked examples. Click Step through it like a debugger under each one and press Step ▶ (or →) one line at a time. Before each step, try to guess the next line yourself.

How to use it tonight: Part 1 is a fast refresh of §2.8–3.6 (about an hour). Part 2 teaches §3.9, §4.1, §3.10 and §3.11 from scratch (about 1½ hours), most points first. Then take the mock midterm. Have paper next to you and write every example down as you step through it; writing it is what makes it stick.

Part 1 · Refresh: §2.8 to §3.6

Lesson 1 · §2.8 The derivative from the definition (10 min)

The derivative f′(x)f'(x)f′(x) is the slope of the curve at xxx. You can't get a slope from one point, so take a second point hhh away, find the slope between them, and let hhh shrink to 0.

The definition
f′(x)=lim⁡h→0f(x+h)−f(x)hf'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}f′(x)=h→0lim​hf(x+h)−f(x)​

Recipe: plug in x+hx+hx+h, subtract f(x)f(x)f(x), cancel what cancels, divide out the hhh, then set h=0h=0h=0.

Tricks

Square roots: multiply by the conjugate. Fractions like 1x\frac1xx1​: use a common denominator. If nothing cancels, you made an algebra mistake.

Lesson 2 · §3.1–3.2 Power, product and quotient rules (10 min)

Power rule
(xn)′=nxn−1(x^n)'=nx^{n-1}(xn)′=nxn−1

“Bring the power down, subtract one.” First rewrite roots and fractions as powers: x=x1/2\sqrt x=x^{1/2}x​=x1/2, 1x2=x−2\frac{1}{x^2}=x^{-2}x21​=x−2.

Product
(fg)′=f′g+fg′(fg)'=f'g+fg'(fg)′=f′g+fg′

“Derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times derivative of the second.”

Quotient
(hilo)′=lo⋅hi′−hi⋅lo′lo2\Big(\frac{hi}{lo}\Big)'=\frac{lo\cdot hi'-hi\cdot lo'}{lo^2}(lohi​)′=lo2lo⋅hi′−hi⋅lo′​

“Low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared.” The order matters because of the minus.

Also

(ex)′=ex(e^x)'=e^x(ex)′=ex. Constants: (c)′=0(c)'=0(c)′=0, (5f)′=5f′(5f)'=5f'(5f)′=5f′.

Lesson 3 · §3.3 Trig derivatives and the trig limit (10 min)

Learn 3, get 6
(sin⁡x)′=cos⁡x(\sin x)'=\cos x(sinx)′=cosx
(tan⁡x)′=sec⁡2x(\tan x)'=\sec^2x(tanx)′=sec2x
(sec⁡x)′=sec⁡xtan⁡x(\sec x)'=\sec x\tan x(secx)′=secxtanx

The co- versions: put “co” on everything and add a minus: (cos⁡x)′=−sin⁡x(\cos x)'=-\sin x(cosx)′=−sinx, (cot⁡x)′=−csc⁡2x(\cot x)'=-\csc^2x(cotx)′=−csc2x, (csc⁡x)′=−csc⁡xcot⁡x(\csc x)'=-\csc x\cot x(cscx)′=−cscxcotx.

The limit
lim⁡θ→0sin⁡θθ=1\lim_{\theta\to0}\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}=1θ→0lim​θsinθ​=1

Only when the angle and the denominator match exactly. Otherwise multiply and divide to make them match.

Lesson 4 · §3.4 The chain rule (10 min)

Chain rule
(f(g(x)))′=f′(g(x))⋅g′(x)\big(f(g(x))\big)'=f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)(f(g(x)))′=f′(g(x))⋅g′(x)

“Derivative of the outside, leave the inside alone, times derivative of the inside.” With more layers, keep multiplying, outside to inside.

Spot the layers

Ask: what would I do last on a calculator? That's the outside. sin⁡2(3x)\sin^2(3x)sin2(3x): last step is squaring, then sin, then 3x3x3x.

Lesson 5 · §3.5 Implicit differentiation (10 min)

Recipe

1. Differentiate both sides with respect to xxx. Every time you differentiate a yyy, multiply by y′y'y′.
2. Move all y′y'y′ terms to one side.
3. Factor out y′y'y′ and divide.

Watch out

xyxyxy needs the product rule: y+xy′y+xy'y+xy′. y2y^2y2 needs the chain rule: 2y y′2y\,y'2yy′. A constant goes to 0.

Lesson 6 · §3.6 Logs and inverse trig (10 min)

Logs
(ln⁡u)′=u′u(\ln u)'=\frac{u'}{u}(lnu)′=uu′​

“Derivative of the inside over the inside.” Other bases: (log⁡bx)′=1xln⁡b(\log_b x)'=\frac{1}{x\ln b}(logb​x)′=xlnb1​, (bx)′=bxln⁡b(b^x)'=b^x\ln b(bx)′=bxlnb.

Inverse trig
(tan⁡−1u)′=u′1+u2(\tan^{-1}u)'=\frac{u'}{1+u^2}(tan−1u)′=1+u2u′​
(sin⁡−1u)′=u′1−u2(\sin^{-1}u)'=\frac{u'}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}(sin−1u)′=1−u2​u′​

cos⁡−1\cos^{-1}cos−1 is the same as sin⁡−1\sin^{-1}sin−1 with a minus.

x to the x

Variable in the base and the exponent: take ln⁡\lnln of both sides first.

Part 2 · Learn: §3.9, §4.1, §3.10, §3.11

These are probably the sections you haven't seen properly yet. They're in order of how many points they're usually worth: related rates and max/min are long, multi-step problems; linear approximation and hyperbolic functions are short ones.

Lesson 7 · §3.9 Related rates (30 min)

The idea: two quantities are connected by an equation, and both are changing over time. You're told how fast one is changing and asked how fast the other is changing at one particular moment.

The key move: differentiate the equation with respect to time ttt. Every changing quantity then picks up its own rate (x→dxdtx\to\frac{dx}{dt}x→dtdx​) by the chain rule. That's the same idea as implicit differentiation, with ttt instead of xxx.

The recipe

1. Draw it. Letters for things that change, numbers for things that don't.
2. Write Given and Want as rates (dxdt=2\frac{dx}{dt}=2dtdx​=2, want dydt\frac{dy}{dt}dtdy​).
3. Write the equation connecting the letters.
4. Differentiate with respect to ttt.
5. Plug in the numbers for this moment and solve.

The equation is usually one of

Pythagoras x2+y2=z2x^2+y^2=z^2x2+y2=z2 (ladders, cars, planes). Sphere V=43πr3V=\frac43\pi r^3V=34​πr3. Cone V=13πr2hV=\frac13\pi r^2hV=31​πr2h. Similar triangles (shadows, cone tanks).

Never plug in early

Plug numbers for changing quantities in only after step 4. Otherwise they become constants, their rates become 0, and the answer is wrong.

Signs

Getting smaller (sliding down, leaking, shrinking) means a negative rate.

Lesson 8 · §4.1 Maximum and minimum values (25 min)

The idea: the highest and lowest points of a graph happen where the graph turns around (slope 0, or a sharp corner where the slope doesn't exist) or at the ends of the interval. So you only need to check a short list of xxx-values.

Absolute max/min = the highest/lowest value on the whole interval. Local max/min = a peak or valley compared with nearby points.

Critical number

A number ccc in the domain of fff where f′(c)=0f'(c)=0f′(c)=0 or f′(c)f'(c)f′(c) doesn't exist.
Find them: compute f′f'f′, write it as one fraction, factor. Top = 0 gives one kind; bottom = 0 gives the other.

Closed Interval Method

For the absolute max and min of fff on [a,b][a,b][a,b]:
1. Find critical numbers; keep only those inside [a,b][a,b][a,b].
2. Make a table: fff at each critical number and at both endpoints aaa, bbb.
3. Largest value = absolute max, smallest = absolute min.

Mistakes that cost points

Evaluating f′f'f′ instead of fff in the table. Forgetting the endpoints. Counting a point where fff itself is undefined.

Lesson 9 · §3.10 Linear approximation and differentials (15 min)

The idea: zoom in close enough on a smooth curve and it looks like a straight line, its tangent line. So near a point you know, use the tangent line to estimate values that are hard to compute by hand, like 4.1\sqrt{4.1}4.1​.

Linearization
L(x)=f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)L(x)=f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)

“Start at the height, move with the slope.” Pick aaa close to your number where f(a)f(a)f(a) is easy.

Differentials
dy=f′(x) dxdy=f'(x)\,dxdy=f′(x)dx

dydydy = change along the tangent line (the estimate). Δy=f(x+dx)−f(x)\Delta y=f(x+dx)-f(x)Δy=f(x+dx)−f(x) = the real change.

Lesson 10 · §3.11 Hyperbolic functions (15 min)

The idea: sinh and cosh aren't new mysteries. They're just names for two combinations of exe^xex and e−xe^{-x}e−x. Every question is either “use the definition” or “use the derivative table”, which looks almost exactly like the trig table.

Definitions
sinh⁡x=ex−e−x2\sinh x=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}{2}sinhx=2ex−e−x​
cosh⁡x=ex+e−x2\cosh x=\frac{e^x+e^{-x}}{2}coshx=2ex+e−x​

sinh has the minus, cosh has the plus. sinh⁡0=0\sinh0=0sinh0=0, cosh⁡0=1\cosh0=1cosh0=1.

Derivatives
(sinh⁡x)′=cosh⁡x(\sinh x)'=\cosh x(sinhx)′=coshx
(cosh⁡x)′=sinh⁡x(\cosh x)'=\sinh x(coshx)′=sinhx
(tanh⁡x)′=sech⁡2x(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x(tanhx)′=sech2x

Like trig, but cosh has no minus.

Identity
cosh⁡2x−sinh⁡2x=1\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1cosh2x−sinh2x=1

A minus, unlike sin⁡2+cos⁡2=1\sin^2+\cos^2=1sin2+cos2=1.

With ln inside

eln⁡a=ae^{\ln a}=aelna=a and e−ln⁡a=1ae^{-\ln a}=\frac1ae−lna=a1​. That's how cosh⁡(ln⁡3)\cosh(\ln 3)cosh(ln3) becomes a plain number.
